title: Healthy lifestyle choices
keyIdea: Everyday choices change how your body works. When you run, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster and you breathe faster. Regular exercise makes the heart muscle stronger, so each beat pumps more blood and the resting heart rate falls. Children need at least 60 active minutes a day on average, and short bursts add up. Free sugar (added sugar, honey, syrup and juice) should stay under 24 g a day at ages 7 to 10, and sugar at fewer times means fewer acid attacks on teeth. Smoke puts carbon monoxide in the blood and tar in the lungs, alcohol harms the liver and a growing brain, and children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep.
familyTip: Find your pulse on the wrist together, count it for 15 seconds and times it by 4. Jog on the spot for a minute and count again. Then look at a can of fizzy drink at home and find how many grams of sugar it has.

visual.caption: Free sugar or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: run and rest, train a heart, build 60 active minutes, keep sugar under 24 g, time sweets for teeth, and breathe smoky air.

kid: Some everyday choices help your body work well. Being active, eating well and sleeping enough all help. So does keeping away from smoke and alcohol. When you run, your muscles need more oxygen. So your heart beats faster and you breathe faster to bring it. When you rest, both slow down again.

Your heart is a muscle, so exercise makes it stronger. A strong heart pumps more blood with each beat. Then it needs fewer beats when you rest. You need at least 60 active minutes a day. Active means you get warm and puff, like on a bike ride. Short bursts add up. Sitting at a screen does not count.

Free sugar is sugar added to food and drinks. Honey, syrup and juice count too. The sugar inside a whole apple is not free sugar, and nor is the sugar in plain milk. At 7 to 10, have no more than 24 g a day. One can of cola has about 35 g. Each time you have sugar, germs on your teeth make acid for up to an hour. So sweets with a meal do less harm than sweets all day.

Smoke from cigarettes has a gas in it called carbon monoxide. It takes the place of oxygen in your blood and will not let go. Tar in smoke clogs up the lungs. Alcohol harms the liver and a growing brain, so the best choice for children is none. Sleep matters too. At your age you need about 9 to 12 hours a night.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This is England's Year 6 science statement 'recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way their bodies function'. It builds on Year 2 (exercise, eating the right amounts of different types of food, and hygiene) and on the Year 6 circulatory system. Key words: lifestyle, heart rate, resting heart rate, circulatory system, free sugars, tooth decay, carbon monoxide, tar, nicotine, addiction.

The UK Chief Medical Officers (2019) ask 5 to 18 year olds for an average of at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a day across the week. The NHS talk test sorts it: moderate means you can talk but not sing, and vigorous means you can only say a few words. During exercise, heart rate and breathing rise to deliver more oxygen. Regular training strengthens the heart, so it pumps more blood per beat and the resting rate falls. The lab's heart rates are example values for a 10-year-old.

Free sugars are sugars added to food and drink, plus those in honey, syrups, juices and smoothies. Sugars inside whole fruit and vegetables and in plain milk are not free sugars. The NHS limits are 19 g a day at 4 to 6, 24 g at 7 to 10 and 30 g from 11, and juice and smoothies together at most 150 ml a day. A 330 ml can of cola has about 35 g. The Oral Health Foundation notes that each sugar intake starts an acid attack of up to an hour, so how often counts more than how much.

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin over 200 times more tightly than oxygen; smokers' blood usually has 3 to 10% of its haemoglobin carrying it instead of oxygen, and heavy smokers up to 15% (RIVM; Blumenthal 2001). Tar clogs the airways, and nicotine is addictive. The Chief Medical Officers advise an alcohol-free childhood. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2016) advises 9 to 12 hours of sleep for ages 6 to 12. Common mistakes: thinking exercise wears the heart out; thinking only one long session counts; counting exciting screen games as active; thinking juice is fine because it is fruit; counting whole fruit as free sugar; thinking small sweets spread through the day are kinder to teeth; and thinking smoking only harms the lungs. In the lab the learner runs and rests, trains a heart for 8 weeks, builds 60 active minutes, picks 4 items under 24 g, times 4 sweets and breathes smoky air.

practice.prompt: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
choices: Your muscles need more oxygen, so more blood must reach them
practice.hint: What do working muscles need more of, and what carries it?
practice.explain: Working muscles use more oxygen. Blood carries it, so the heart beats faster to send more blood.

practice.prompt: You walk to school for {a} minutes and play tag for {b} minutes. How many more active minutes do you need to reach 60?
practice.hint: Add the two active times, then take the total away from 60.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} active minutes, so you need 60 − {=a+b} = {=60-a-b} more.

practice.prompt: At ages 7 to 10 the limit is 24 g of free sugar a day. A child drinks a juice with {a} g. How many grams are left for the rest of the day?
practice.hint: Juice sugar is free sugar. Take it away from 24.
practice.explain: 24 − {a} = {=24-a} g of free sugar left for the day.

practice.prompt: Which plan gives your teeth the fewest acid attacks?
choices: Eat the sweets all together after lunch
Suck one sweet slowly all afternoon
practice.hint: Each time sugar goes in, acid attacks teeth for up to an hour.
practice.explain: All together after lunch is one sugar time, so one acid attack. Spreading them out makes many attacks.

practice.prompt: What does carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke do?
choices: It takes the place of oxygen in red blood cells
It makes the blood carry more oxygen
practice.hint: Think about the seats on the red blood cells in the lab.
practice.explain: Carbon monoxide grabs the seats where oxygen should ride and holds on tightly, so less oxygen reaches the body.

pool.prompt: Each time you have something sugary, your teeth are under acid attack for up to an hour. You have sugary snacks at {a} different times today. Up to how many hours of acid attack is that?
pool.hint: Count one attack of up to an hour for each sugar time.
pool.explain: {a} sugar times means up to {a} hours of acid attack. Fewer sugar times means fewer attacks.

pool.prompt: A resting heart beats {a} times a minute. How many times does it beat in {b} minutes?
pool.hint: Multiply the beats in one minute by the number of minutes.

pool.prompt: Someone is active every day for months. What happens to their resting heart rate?
choices: It goes up, because the heart is worn out
pool.hint: A stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat.
pool.explain: Exercise strengthens the heart, so each beat pumps more blood and fewer beats are needed at rest.

pool.prompt: Which of these counts towards your 60 active minutes?
choices: An hour of an exciting video game
Watching a football match on TV
pool.hint: Active time makes you warm and out of breath.
pool.explain: The bike ride makes you puff, so it counts. Screen time is sitting time, however exciting it is.

pool.prompt: Which has free sugar that counts towards the 24 g limit?
pool.hint: Juicing breaks open the fruit and frees its sugar.
pool.explain: Juice sugar is free sugar. The sugar inside a whole orange and in plain milk is not.

pool.prompt: A 330 ml can of cola has about 35 g of sugar. For a 9-year-old, that is…
choices: more than the whole day's 24 g
about a quarter of the day's limit
fine, because it is a drink
pool.hint: Compare 35 g with the 24 g limit for ages 7 to 10.
pool.explain: 35 g is more than 24 g, so one can goes over the whole day's limit.

choices: the lungs, the heart and the blood
only people who smoke a lot
pool.hint: Think about tar in the lungs and carbon monoxide in the blood.
pool.explain: Tar clogs the lungs, carbon monoxide takes oxygen's place in the blood, and the heart has to work harder.

pool.prompt: About how much sleep does a 10-year-old need each night?
pool.hint: Children aged 6 to 12 need more sleep than adults.
pool.explain: Sleep experts advise 9 to 12 hours a night for children aged 6 to 12.

pool.prompt: What do the UK's top doctors say is the healthiest choice about alcohol for children?
pool.hint: Alcohol harms the liver and a brain that is still growing.
pool.explain: The Chief Medical Officers advise an alcohol-free childhood, because alcohol harms the liver and the growing brain.
